title: Sympathy: title and occasion
short: Published in Lyrics of the Hearthside (1899); his widow said the iron grilles of the Library of Congress stacks, where he worked from 1897, suggested the bird's cage.
body: Dunbar (1872-1906), the son of formerly enslaved parents, took a post as an attendant at the Library of Congress in Washington on 30 September 1897; the work among the stacks, in summer heat, was unhealthy and confining. In 1914 his widow, Alice Dunbar Nelson, wrote that the iron grating of the book stacks suggested to him the bars of a bird's cage. The poem appeared in Lyrics of the Hearthside (1899). The title, from Greek sympatheia, 'feeling with', claims the speaker's suffering is the bird's: he does not pity it from outside but knows it from within. The bird has been read as figuring the condition of Black Americans after slavery, and of the artist constrained by a racist culture.

title: the refrain 'I know ...'
short: Each stanza opens and closes with 'I know', and the verb that follows changes: what the bird feels, why it beats its wing, why it sings.
body: The refrain frames every stanza and develops through the poem: 'what the caged bird feels' (st. 1), 'why the caged bird beats his wing' (st. 2), 'why the caged bird sings' (st. 3). The progression moves from feeling to action to art, and the final stanza's revelation is that singing is a form of the same struggle as beating against the bars. The insistent first person 'I know' asserts experience rather than observation, which gives the poem its moral authority. Maya Angelou took the title of her autobiography, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969), from the final line.

sources.cite: Joanne M. Braxton, ed., The Collected Poetry of Paul Laurence Dunbar (UP of Virginia, 1993), introduction and notes

title: Stanza and rhyme
short: Three seven-line stanzas with indented b-lines and a shortened refrain; stanzas 1 and 3 rhyme abaabcc, stanza 2 abaabaa; the rhythm mixes iambs and anapaests.
body: The first stanza rhymes abaabcc (alas/slopes/grass/glass/opes/steals/feels), as does the third (me/sore/free/glee/core/flings/sings); the second rhymes abaabaa, because the c-rhyme is replaced by the -ing of 'wing' (wing/bars/cling/swing/scars/sting/wing). The b-lines are indented, and the closing line is a shortened echo of the first. The lines are mostly four-stress, mixing iambic and anapaestic feet ('When the WIND stirs SOFT through the SPRINGing GRASS'), a lilting movement that suits song and also suggests the bird's beating. Keith Leonard has noted that the poem follows Standard English norms, unlike Dunbar's dialect verse, and links its celebration of nature to the Romantic poets, while arguing that it also betrays Dunbar's social anxieties.

sources.cite: Joanne M. Braxton, ed., The Collected Poetry of Paul Laurence Dunbar (UP of Virginia, 1993), introduction and notes

title: upland
short: High ground, hill country; the open landscape the bird can see but not reach.
body: 'Upland' denotes higher ground, away from towns and rivers, and in poetic diction it suggests freedom and fresh air. The first stanza is a catalogue of a spring day seen from inside the cage: sun, wind, grass, river, the first song and first bud. The pain lies in the contrast between the bird's confinement and the visible, unreachable world. The springtime setting may also hint at the hopes of Emancipation and Reconstruction, which by the 1890s had been betrayed.

title: springing
short: Sprouting, growing fresh; the grass of spring, with a pun on the season.
body: To 'spring' is to rise or sprout, and the participle describes young grass shooting up in spring. The word also suggests leaping and elasticity, qualities denied the caged bird. The repeated 'When' clauses accumulate the season's freedoms, each one a reproach to the cage. The participle also keeps the scene in motion: the grass is still growing, the wind still stirring, the river still flowing, while the bird alone is fixed in place. Dunbar's nature catalogue thus works by contrast rather than celebration.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'springing, adj.'

title: a stream of glass
short: A clear, smooth river flowing like glass; a tranquil image, but glass is also the hard, transparent substance that separates viewer and world.
body: The simile pictures a slow, transparent river, smooth as glass. Some readers have noticed the irony: glass, like the bars of a cage, is a barrier through which one can see without passing; the transparency of the world outside makes the bird's exclusion sharper. The figure is a conventional poetic one (compare Milton's 'glassy, cool, translucent wave' in Comus, l. 861), and its conventionality is part of the stanza's deliberate idyllic surface.

sources.cite: John Milton, A Mask (Comus) (1634), l. 861
Joanne M. Braxton, ed., The Collected Poetry of Paul Laurence Dunbar (UP of Virginia, 1993), introduction and notes

title: opes
short: Archaic poetic form of 'opens'; the first flower bud of spring unfolding.
body: 'Ope' is an archaic and poetic short form of 'open', common in Romantic and Victorian verse ('ope their golden eyes', Cymbeline 2.3). Dunbar's standard-English poems often use such literary diction, consciously placing himself in the line of English lyric. The 'first bird sings and the first bud opes' marks the very beginning of spring, the season of renewal the caged bird cannot share.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'ope, v.'
William Shakespeare, Cymbeline, 2.3.22

title: chalice
short: The cup-shaped flower, likened to the chalice of the Eucharist, from which scent drifts out; 'steals' means moves softly, unseen.
body: A chalice is a drinking cup, especially the cup of wine in the Christian Eucharist, and by extension a cup-shaped flower (Latin calix also gives 'calyx'). The religious overtone anticipates the poem's close, in which the bird's song becomes a prayer to Heaven. 'Steals' means slips quietly away, and the scent escaping from the flower is a free movement the bird cannot imitate.

title: blood on the cruel bars
short: The bird beats against its cage until it bleeds; a violent image of the cost of resistance.
body: The second stanza moves from longing to struggle. The bird's beating of its wing against the bars until 'its blood is red' is the poem's most violent image, and the transferred epithet 'cruel' gives the bars a will of their own. The image belongs to a long tradition of caged birds as figures of the captive spirit, from Sterne's starling in A Sentimental Journey (1768), whose 'I can't get out' made Yorick reflect on slavery and imprisonment, to many nineteenth-century anti-slavery poems. Dunbar gives the tradition a first-person, racial urgency.

sources.cite: Laurence Sterne, A Sentimental Journey through France and Italy (1768), 'The Passport. The Hotel at Paris' (the starling)

title: fain
short: Archaic: gladly, willingly; 'would fain be' means 'would gladly be' or 'longs to be'.
body: 'Fain' (Old English faegen, 'glad') survives chiefly in the archaic phrase 'would fain', meaning 'would gladly' or 'wishes to'. The line contrasts the forced return to the perch, where the bird must 'cling', with the swinging bough where it longs to be. 'A-swing' uses the old prefix a- (from 'on'), as in 'a-hunting', for an ongoing action; the swaying bough is free motion, the perch is fixed.

title: the old, old scars
short: The bird's old wounds reopen at each new struggle; many readers take them as the inherited wounds of slavery.
body: The doubled 'old, old' suggests wounds received long before, which 'pulse again with a keener sting' at each new effort. Read historically, the old scars are those of slavery, from which Dunbar's parents had escaped or been freed (his father, Joshua Dunbar, escaped slavery and served in the Union army), and the new sting is the racism of the 1890s, the decade of segregation laws, disfranchisement and lynching. Read more personally, they are the frustrations of an artist who felt confined by the expectation that he write dialect verse. The poem supports both readings; Christine Wooley argues that Dunbar identifies with the bird but shifts attention, in the last stanza, to the song itself.

sources.cite: Joanne M. Braxton, ed., The Collected Poetry of Paul Laurence Dunbar (UP of Virginia, 1993), introduction and notes

title: carol
greek: Old French carole, a ring-dance with song
short: A joyful song (originally a song for a ring-dance); the bird's singing is mistaken by hearers for happiness.
body: A carol was originally a song accompanying a ring-dance (Old French carole), then any joyful song, especially at Christmas. The final stanza corrects a misreading: listeners assume the caged bird sings because it is happy, but its song is a prayer and a plea. Critics have connected this with the minstrel stereotype of the 'happy' singing slave and with white readers' reception of Black art as entertainment; it also bears on Dunbar's own reputation for cheerful dialect poems, which he felt obscured his serious verse (compare 'We Wear the Mask', 1895).

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'carol, n.'

anchor: But a prayer that he sends
title: a prayer ... a plea
short: The song is a prayer from the heart's core and a plea flung upward to Heaven: art as petition for freedom.
body: The climax redefines the song as prayer and plea, directed 'upward to Heaven'. The vertical movement contrasts with the horizontal bars: the bird cannot fly, but its voice can rise. The language echoes the spirituals, in which song itself was a coded petition for deliverance, and gives the poem a religious resolution without any assurance that the prayer will be answered. 'Flings' recalls the beating wing: singing is a form of struggle, not consolation.
